newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Air Force orders flight changes in the skies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Air Force orders flight changes in the skies.

text.p: The Air Force said on Tuesday its fighter jets have been ordered to stay away from civilian airliners, but bluntly denied any showing off by an F-16 pilot in a recent close encounter intercept off New Jersey.

Air Force Maj. Gen. Donald Peterson told reporters that Air Force jets on training manoeuvres had been told to stay at least 5,000 feet (1,524 metres) horizontally and 1,000 feet (305 metres) vertically away from airliners in the future.

The step followed four recent near-miss encounters between civilian planes and F-16s, including one on Feb. 5 in which a New Jersey Air National Guard jet pulled within 1,000 feet (305 metres) of a Nations Air Boeing 727, triggering the 727's crash warning system and causing its pilot to manuever sharply.
Two flight attendants and a passenger were thrown to the cabin floor in the incident off the New Jersey coast.

But Peterson termed irresponsible suggestions by some critics that the fighter pilot in the Nations Air incident as well as other military pilots were sometimes guilty of "hot-dogging" by "tail-gating" civilian aircraft too closely.
"We just don't accept hot-dogging. This is not World War II," he told a Pentagon news conference. "Fun and flying in the area of airliners is not part of our syllabus."
Peterson, an assistant deputy Air Force chief of staff, said any discipline of military pilots in the four incidents, which occurred over a two-day period, would be up to local commanders.

The National Transportation Safety Board, which held a separate news conference on Tuesday, denied there had been an epidemic of near-misses in the nation's airways but said the Feb. 5 incident needed more investigation.
That incident clearly raised potential safety concerns, NTSB officials said.
They indicated investigators were focusing on an apparent breakdown in communications between military air traffic controllers and the pilots of one of a flight of two F-16 fighter jets in the area.
"The potential for very unfortunate results was clearly there," Jim Hall, chairman of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), told a news conference.
"There clearly was miscommunication or a lack of communication between military air controllers and the flight of F-16s," Hall said.

"Our investigation continues. The military has implemented procedural changes," Hall said, adding that the safety board expected its own investigators to provide it with further safety recommendations within the next 10 days.
